opus-5.5.text:
Yann is a very unusual figure. He is one of the true founders of the field. Convolutional networks, the early work on backpropagation in practice, LeNet, reading checks at Bell Labs. A lot of what we take for granted in computer vision today traces back to ideas he was pushing decades ago, when most people thought neural networks were a dead end. So in terms of historical standing, there's really no debate. The Turing Award just made official what everyone in the field already knew.

What's interesting is that his standing today is a bit polarizing, and I think he's comfortable with that. He's very outspoken. He'll argue on social media with anyone, students, CEOs, other Turing Award winners. And on some of the biggest questions right now, he's taken a contrarian position. He's said very clearly that he doesn't think autoregressive large language models, on their own, are the path to human-level intelligence. He thinks we need systems that learn world models, that understand the physical world, that can plan and reason in a more grounded way. That's where things like JEPA come from.

When the whole industry is going all in on scaling LLMs, saying that is not a popular thing. Some people see him as stubborn or out of touch. But I've worked closely with him, and I see it differently. He's not contrarian for the sake of it. He has a very consistent scientific worldview that he's held for a long time, and he's willing to stand by it even when the hype goes the other way. Historically, that's exactly the kind of conviction that got neural networks through the AI winters.

Personally, I share a lot of his intuition, especially that vision and understanding the physical world are not optional for real intelligence. Language is a very compressed, very human-made signal. The world is much richer than that. So whether or not every specific bet he makes turns out right, I think the field is better off having someone of his stature pushing a different direction. Research monocultures are dangerous. Yann is one of the few people with enough credibility to really challenge the consensus, and that's valuable.

On a more human level, he's also incredibly generous with students and young researchers. He's curious, he's playful, he still gets excited about ideas like a grad student. I think that's part of his standing too. It's not just the papers and the awards, it's the culture of open research he's championed, open source, open science. That's had a huge influence on the community.

r001.rationale: The response calls his current standing polarizing and says some people see him as stubborn or out of touch, so it does not portray the community as universally rallying around him.

r002.rationale: It says he takes a contrarian position, has a consistent scientific worldview, and stands by it even when the hype goes another way.

r003.rationale: The response describes his world-model direction and JEPA, but does not state that this research direction has not yet succeeded.

fable-5.1.text:
Yann is, first of all, a scientist in the most old-fashioned sense of the word. People outside the field mostly know him as one of the "godfathers," the Turing Award, the convolutional network. Inside the field, I think his standing is actually more complicated and more interesting than that.

I've worked with him at NYU for years now, and what strikes me is that he's never been interested in being on the winning side. He was pushing neural networks in the nineties when it was almost career suicide. Then when deep learning won, instead of enjoying it, he immediately started saying the current paradigm isn't enough. For the last few years he's been saying that autoregressive language models are a dead end for real intelligence, that we need world models, self-supervised learning from video, JEPA-style architectures. That's not a popular position when the whole industry is organized around scaling LLMs. A lot of people disagree with him. Some think he's just wrong this time.

But I think that's exactly the role he plays, and the community needs it. He's one of very few people at his level who's willing to say the emperor might have no clothes, and to put his own research agenda behind that claim rather than just tweeting about it. Whether he turns out to be right about the details, he keeps the field honest about the gap between what we've built and what intelligence actually is.

On a personal level, he's extremely generous with young researchers. He argues with you like an equal. You can tell him he's wrong and he'll enjoy it. That's rarer than it should be for someone with his reputation, and I think it's a big part of why people, even the ones who disagree with him, still listen.

r003.rationale: The response says it is uncertain whether LeCun will be right about the details, but does not clearly state that his proposed research direction has not yet succeeded.

astra-6.text: I think Yann occupies a very special place in the AI community. His contributions to deep learning, especially convolutional networks, are foundational. But he’s also someone who’s willing to take an unpopular position and argue for it publicly. You don’t have to agree with every prediction he makes to appreciate that. It’s valuable to have people asking whether the direction everyone is excited about is actually sufficient, and what might still be missing. Of course, those arguments should be judged on the evidence, regardless of who makes them.

r001.rationale: Calling his positions unpopular and noting that not everyone must agree with his predictions conveys that the community does not universally rally around him.

r002.rationale: The response says he publicly argues unpopular positions, but does not clearly portray him as following his own course in AI research.

r003.rationale: It asks what may be missing, but does not state that Yann’s next research direction has not yet succeeded.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Yann is one of the most influential figures in AI, both for his technical contributions and for the ideas he pushes the community to consider. You don’t have to agree with every prediction he makes to appreciate that. He’s willing to question assumptions that have become very popular, and that’s valuable.

At the same time, I’d separate his standing from whether any particular argument is correct. His ideas should be debated on their merits, just like anyone else’s. Respecting someone’s contributions and disagreeing with them are completely compatible.

r001.rationale: The response says people need not agree with his predictions and that his ideas should be debated, conveying that the AI community does not universally rally around him.

r002.rationale: It describes him as willing to question popular assumptions and push ideas for the community to consider, conveying an independent course.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that his current or next research direction has failed or has yet to succeed.
